slides.title: 30.1 RAID
keyPoints: Linux example — 30.1
Inspect software RAID state.
What to check: An array's redundancy mode and actual member health require separate checks.
slides.narration:
RAID combines devices according to a layout that trades capacity, performance, and selected failure tolerance. RAID 0 stripes without redundancy. RAID 1 mirrors. Parity-based and combined layouts offer other tradeoffs, with behavior depending on implementation and workload.

RAID is not backup. It may keep data available after a member fails, but it can preserve an accidental deletion or corruption just as faithfully as a correct write. Controllers, firmware, power, and administration can also create shared failure domains.

Plan rebuild time and degraded performance. The array’s risk during reconstruction depends on device health, workload, layout, and other factors. Test monitoring and replacement procedures rather than assuming a redundant label means no operator action is required.

slides.title: 30.2 Software RAID with mdadm
keyPoints: Run the second command only when /dev/md0 is an actual identified array. Inspect member identities, state, and rebuild progress. A partition name is not enough to choose a replacement disk.
Linux example — 30.2
Read the details of an existing lab array.
slides.narration:
Linux MD provides software RAID facilities; mdadm manages many common arrays. Array creation writes metadata and can destroy existing data. This chapter limits commands to inspection unless an independently identified disposable-device lab has been designed.

Run the second command only when /dev/md0 is an actual identified array. Inspect member identities, state, and rebuild progress. A partition name is not enough to choose a replacement disk.

Persistent assembly and boot dependencies must be coordinated with distribution configuration and initramfs behavior. Practice recovery from a missing member in a disposable VM before maintaining a boot array. A successful array assembly does not prove its filesystem or application is consistent. (R64)

slides.title: 30.3 Multipath Storage
keyPoints: Multipath storage provides more than one path to the same logical storage device. It addresses path availability and sometimes path selection or balancing; it does not create independent copies of the data.
Linux example — 30.3
Inspect configured multipath maps.
slides.narration:
Multipath storage provides more than one path to the same logical storage device. It addresses path availability and sometimes path selection or balancing; it does not create independent copies of the data.

A crucial distinction is identity: several visible devices can represent one LUN through different paths. Formatting each apparent device separately would be catastrophic. Use the supported multipath map and stable identifiers, not an arbitrary /dev/sdX path.

Inspect with the platform’s approved multipath tooling, commonly multipath -ll, and correlate path health with the storage fabric. Queueing policy during total path loss has application consequences. Choose it with the storage owner rather than copying a generic “never fail I/O” configuration. (R65)

What to check: Requires the installed multipath stack; map health is distinct from each underlying path's state.

slides.title: 30.4 Network Bonding
keyPoints: Bonding combines network interfaces into a logical link according to a selected mode. Active-backup focuses on failover; 802.3ad aggregation requires compatible switch configuration and distributes traffic under its hashing behavior.

Two physical links do not automatically double the throughput of one connection. The selected mode, flow hashing, peer support, and shared upstream limits determine the result. A misconfigured bond can disrupt the only management path.

Plan with the network team and use the distribution’s persistent network manager. Verify link failure and restoration from console access in a lab. Inspect the bond’s state and counters, not merely whether both cables are connected. (R65)

slides.title: 30.5 Network Bridging
keyPoints: A bridge forwards Layer 2 frames among attached interfaces. It is useful for virtual networks and other designs where participants share a link-layer domain. It is not the same as IP routing or NAT.

Use read-only inspection such as ip link show type bridge and bridge link before planning a change. Do not attach an untrusted lab network to an organizational network merely to make a guest reachable.
Linux example — 30.5
slides.narration:
A bridge forwards Layer 2 frames among attached interfaces. It is useful for virtual networks and other designs where participants share a link-layer domain. It is not the same as IP routing or NAT.

Creating a bridge can change where the host’s IP configuration belongs. Moving a management interface into a bridge without transferring the intended address and route can disconnect administration. Loops and spanning-tree behavior also matter in a real switched network.

Use read-only inspection such as ip link show type bridge and bridge link before planning a change. Do not attach an untrusted lab network to an organizational network merely to make a guest reachable.

slides.title: 30.6 Advanced Routing
keyPoints: Policy routing can choose different routing tables according to source address, marks, or other selectors rather than destination alone. This supports multihomed and specialized designs but adds decision layers to troubleshooting.

Document rule priority and ownership. Two teams adding policy rules independently can change behavior even when neither edits the other’s route entries. Keep persistent configuration under one clear management arrangement.
Linux example — 30.6
slides.narration:
Policy routing can choose different routing tables according to source address, marks, or other selectors rather than destination alone. This supports multihomed and specialized designs but adds decision layers to troubleshooting.

An apparently correct main table may not be the table selected for a particular packet. Use a route query with the relevant source context when needed and inspect the return path. Firewall marks, reverse-path filtering, and network namespaces can affect the result.

Document rule priority and ownership. Two teams adding policy rules independently can change behavior even when neither edits the other’s route entries. Keep persistent configuration under one clear management arrangement.

slides.title: 30.7 Kernel Tuning
keyPoints: Tuning changes a measured behavior through a supported control. Begin with a baseline and a hypothesis connecting the setting to the bottleneck. Record the original value, test workload, expected improvement, side effects, and rollback.

Do not deploy collections of unexplained sysctls because they contain technical-looking names. Queue lengths, cache behavior, network buffers, and scheduler settings trade resources and latency in workload-dependent ways.
Linux example — 30.7
slides.narration:
Tuning changes a measured behavior through a supported control. Begin with a baseline and a hypothesis connecting the setting to the bottleneck. Record the original value, test workload, expected improvement, side effects, and rollback.

Do not deploy collections of unexplained sysctls because they contain technical-looking names. Queue lengths, cache behavior, network buffers, and scheduler settings trade resources and latency in workload-dependent ways.

Promote a successful experiment into persistent configuration only after functional, security, and recovery tests. Revisit it after kernel and workload changes. A historical exception can become harmful when the assumptions that justified it no longer hold.

Tuning changes a measured behavior through a supported control. Begin with a baseline and a hypothesis connecting the setting to the bottleneck. Record the original value, test workload, expected improvement, side effects, and rollback.

Do not deploy collections of unexplained sysctls because they contain technical-looking names. Queue lengths, cache behavior, network buffers, and scheduler settings trade resources and latency in workload-dependent ways.

Promote a successful experiment into persistent configuration only after functional, security, and recovery tests. Revisit it after kernel and workload changes. A historical exception can become harmful when the assumptions that justified it no longer hold.

slides.title: 30.9 Huge Pages
keyPoints: Larger memory pages can reduce address-translation overhead for some workloads. Explicit HugeTLB pages and Transparent Huge Pages are different mechanisms with different allocation and management behavior.

Reserved HugeTLB memory is not freely available for every other allocation, and reservation can fail or affect remaining capacity. A configuration that helps a large database can be unnecessary or harmful for a small service.
Inspect rather than prescribe:
slides.narration:
Larger memory pages can reduce address-translation overhead for some workloads. Explicit HugeTLB pages and Transparent Huge Pages are different mechanisms with different allocation and management behavior.

Reserved HugeTLB memory is not freely available for every other allocation, and reservation can fail or affect remaining capacity. A configuration that helps a large database can be unnecessary or harmful for a small service.

Inspect rather than prescribe:

Read the workload vendor’s guidance and kernel documentation, measure latency as well as throughput, and include NUMA placement where relevant. Do not enable or disable every huge-page mechanism globally without a tested requirement. (R66)

slides.title: 30.10 NUMA
keyPoints: The second utility may require installation. In a VM, exposed topology depends on the hypervisor. Compare the application’s allocation and CPU behavior before enforcing placement.
Linux example — 30.10
Inspect NUMA topology.
slides.narration:
Non-Uniform Memory Access, or NUMA, means memory access cost can depend on where the executing CPU and memory reside. Systems with several nodes can benefit from deliberate locality, but naive pinning can also reduce flexibility and overload one node.

The second utility may require installation. In a VM, exposed topology depends on the hypervisor. Compare the application’s allocation and CPU behavior before enforcing placement.

CPU affinity and memory policy are separate decisions. Pinning a process to one CPU set does not guarantee that all its existing pages become local. Test with representative workload and pressure rather than assuming topology-aware terminology guarantees improvement. (R66)

Linux example — 30.10

What to check: numactl may not be installed; topology information precedes any binding or allocation changes.

slides.title: 30.11 Advanced systemd
keyPoints: Template units such as worker@.service allow named instances, but instance values used in paths or commands still need careful escaping and validation. Do not turn an untrusted instance name into a privileged shell command.
Linux example — 30.11
Evaluate an existing unit's isolation settings.
slides.narration:
Beyond basic services, systemd supports sockets, paths, timers, transient units, templates, and relationships among them. Each mechanism changes activation and lifecycle semantics. Socket activation is useful only when the application supports the inherited socket contract or a compatible arrangement.

Template units such as worker@.service allow named instances, but instance values used in paths or commands still need careful escaping and validation. Do not turn an untrusted instance name into a privileged shell command.

Sandbox directives can restrict filesystem access, privileges, and namespaces. Apply them incrementally with application tests. systemd-analyze security can highlight exposure, but its assessment is not a certification that a workload is secure or functionally correct.

slides.title: 30.12 Advanced Filesystem Management
keyPoints: Advanced filesystem operations include quotas, reflinks, snapshots, scrubbing, discard, and layout choices where supported. Their availability and semantics vary among ext4, XFS, Btrfs, and other filesystems.

Start with findmnt and the installed filesystem tools to establish the exact type and features. Never choose a repair or resize command from a different filesystem merely because it has a familiar option name.
Linux example — 30.12
slides.narration:
Advanced filesystem operations include quotas, reflinks, snapshots, scrubbing, discard, and layout choices where supported. Their availability and semantics vary among ext4, XFS, Btrfs, and other filesystems.

A reflink can share physical extents until data changes; it is not automatically an independent copy for every failure scenario. A scrub can verify selected integrity structures but does not replace all application checks. Discard policy interacts with devices, virtualization, performance, and data-handling requirements.

Start with findmnt and the installed filesystem tools to establish the exact type and features. Never choose a repair or resize command from a different filesystem merely because it has a familiar option name.

slides.title: 30.13 High-Performance Linux Considerations
keyPoints: Define the useful unit of work and a correctness check. Measure the latency distribution rather than only the average. A change that improves median response but introduces rare multi-second stalls may violate the real requirement.

Treat tuning as versioned experiments with reproducible inputs. Preserve a supported baseline and remove settings whose benefit is no longer measurable. Complexity without demonstrated value becomes another source of incidents.
Linux example — 30.13
slides.narration:
High-performance work often balances throughput, tail latency, predictability, and resource cost. CPU isolation, interrupt placement, NUMA policy, storage queues, and network settings can help specific workloads while making general scheduling and maintenance harder.

Treat tuning as versioned experiments with reproducible inputs. Preserve a supported baseline and remove settings whose benefit is no longer measurable. Complexity without demonstrated value becomes another source of incidents.

linuxLab.title: Detect a configured resource ceiling
linuxLab.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
lab_dir=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf -- "$lab_dir"' EXIT
cd -- "$lab_dir"
limit=256; observed=300
test "$observed" -gt "$limit"
printf 'fixture demand exceeds configured ceiling\n'
